title: The wooden bomber flies

facts.text: At 3:45 p.m. on 25 November 1940, the prototype de Havilland Mosquito lifted off from Hatfield, north of London, flown by the company's chief test pilot, Geoffrey de Havilland Jr., with engine designer John E. Walker aboard. The test flight lasted about half an hour.

The Mosquito was built almost entirely of wood, with a fuselage of plywood skins over balsa, a method the designers argued saved weight and speeded production. Pilots came to call it the Wooden Wonder.

It was designed as a fast bomber with no defensive guns at all, on the bet that speed would protect it better than turrets. The Air Ministry doubted it, and Lord Beaverbrook called it "Freeman's Folly" after Air Chief Marshal Sir Wilfrid Freeman, who backed it.

To keep it secret, the prototype was designed and built at Salisbury Hall, about six and a half miles from the Hatfield factory. Construction began in March 1940, and it was taken to Hatfield by road in November, painted all over in trainer yellow.
It flew with two Rolls-Royce Merlin 21 engines and weighed 14,150 lb.
In trials at Boscombe Down in February 1941 it reached 392 mph at 22,000 feet, faster than the Spitfires of the day.
Testing was not smooth. On 24 February 1941 its tailwheel jammed while taxiing and the fuselage broke; it was repaired with the fuselage of the second prototype.
"Freeman's Folly" became one of the most versatile aircraft of the war, flying as a bomber, night fighter, fighter bomber and photo reconnaissance plane. 7,781 were built.
Geoffrey de Havilland Jr. did not see the jet age through. On 27 September 1946 his DH 108 jet broke up over the Thames Estuary during high speed tests, and he was killed.

photoNote: Tier: green, with a provenance caveat. The prototype W4050 taking off or landing on grass, serial W4050 and roundel clear, side view. Commons file tagged PD UK Government (Crown copyright expired, photo before 1957), source given only as "British RAF", unknown photographer; the Commons page dates it to the maiden flight of 25 November 1940, which I could not confirm (People's Mosquito says it flew that day in all over trainer yellow, and the serial and roundel are visible here), so credit it as 1940 to 1941. 1079 x 568, the largest copy on Commons; meets the 960 px minimum. Runner up: Mosquito B Mk IV Series 2 DK338 in flight, November 1942, IWM CH 7781, Crown copyright expired, 1300 x 965 (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:De_Havilland_Mosquito-DK338-1942.jpg), an early bomber with a firmer IWM number if Brian prefers it.
photoCredit: The Mosquito prototype W4050 at Hatfield, 1940 to 1941. Crown copyright expired, public domain (Wikimedia Commons).

declassified.fact: W4050 still exists. After years in storage at Hatfield and elsewhere it went back to Salisbury Hall, the manor where it was secretly built, and has been preserved there since 1959 at what is now the de Havilland Aircraft Museum.

body:
Lord Beaverbrook called it "Freeman's Folly": a bomber with no guns at all, built almost entirely of wood.

25 November 1940. At 3:45 p.m. Geoffrey de Havilland Jr. took the yellow prototype up from Hatfield, with engine designer John E. Walker aboard, for about half an hour. It had been built in secret at Salisbury Hall and brought to the airfield by road.

The bet was that speed would protect it better than turrets. In trials in February 1941 it reached 392 mph at 22,000 feet, faster than the Spitfires of the day.

The folly became a bomber, night fighter, fighter bomber and reconnaissance plane, and 7,781 were built. De Havilland himself died in 1946 when his DH 108 jet broke up over the Thames Estuary.
